full_judgment:
3. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The learned Assistant Judge by judgment and decree dated 9.7.84 decreed the suit on contest against defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and ex pert against the rest. The contesting defendants filed an appeal Other Appeal No. 499/84, from the said judgment and decree. It was contended by them in the appeal that defendant Nos. 7-9 (respondents 6-8 herein) who were minors were not represented by any guardian in the trial court. On behalf of the plaintiffs it was submitted that no relief was prayed for against the said minor defendants and a Court guardian for the said minors having been appointed in the appellate court, the irregularity, if any, at the trial stage was cured. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, being of the view that non-compliance of the provision of Order 32, rule 3 C. P. C by the trial court was not curable, passed an order of remand on 8 July 1986 without entering into the merit of the case. This order of remand was challenged before the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench, in Civil Revision No. 318 of 1986. A Single Judge, by the impugned Judgment and order dated 2 February 1988, upheld the order of remand and discharged the rule in the said revision case. 

 6. It is an admitted fact that defendants 7-9 (respondent 6-8 herein) were minors during the trial stage and neither their natural guardian appeared nor any court guardian was appointed on their behalf to represent their case, if any. The learned Judge of the High Court Division is right in holding that the provisions of rule 3 of Order 32 C. P. C. which provides for appointment of guardian by court for minor defendants is mandatory but it seems that it has been a too broadly stated by the learned Judge that noncompliance with the aforesaid rule will render the whole proceeding of the suit including the passing of the decree a nullity even if it is found that such noncompliance has not virtually prejudiced the defence of the minor in any way. The cases referred to and relied upon show that the decrees in those cases were being challenged by the minors themselves on the ground that they were not properly represented at the passing of the said decrees and such decrees have been held to be viod. There cannot be any dispute with this proposition. But the facts of the instant case, it will be presently seen, provide a typical example where the decree passed could not be said to be a nullity as a whole even though the court did not appoint a guardian for the minors at the trial. We have seen the plaint and found that relief had been prayed for only against defendants 1-4 who are the principal defendants in the suit. Defendants 5-9 including the minors (nos. 7-9) were made proforma defendants and no relief was claimed against them. The decree passed in the suit could not, therefore, be said to be a nullity as a whole; but since the minor defendants were not properly represented they were neither bound nor any of their interest could be affected by the said decree.
